lessons.title: Chromosomes, DNA and chromosome sets
lessons.question: What exactly are we counting in a cell-division diagram?
lessons.goal: Distinguish chromatin, chromosomes, homologous chromosomes and chromosome sets.
lessons.prior: DNA carries inherited information. A gamete contributes one chromosome set at fertilization.

sections: The genetic material can be packaged differently

DNA associates with proteins to form chromatin. During much of a cell's life, this material is less condensed. As a cell prepares to divide, the DNA becomes more tightly organized into visible chromosomes. Condensation helps the cell move and separate its genetic material without leaving it as a tangled mass.

The chromosome is not created from nothing when it becomes visible. The same genetic material is being packaged differently. Likewise, an uncondensed nucleus has DNA even when you cannot identify individual chromosomes in a light-microscope image.
One type from each parent forms a homologous pair

A typical human body cell has 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs. Most pairs are homologous: the two chromosomes have the same genes at corresponding positions. One typically comes from the mother and one from the father. The alleles, or versions of those genes, need not be identical.

The sex chromosomes require care. In an XX pair the chromosomes are homologous; X and Y share some corresponding regions but are not matching copies over their whole lengths. Autosomes are the chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes.

A karyotype arranges photographed chromosomes by size and other features. It helps examine chromosome number and larger structural differences; it does not directly reveal every DNA sequence or every possible genetic condition.
Sets and copies answer different questions

A haploid cell contains one chromosome set, represented by n. A diploid cell contains two sets, represented by 2n. Human gametes are normally haploid with 23 chromosomes, while the zygote and most body cells are diploid with 46.

Ploidy refers to chromosome sets, not how tightly DNA is packed or whether a chromosome has replicated. A chromosome may be drawn as a single rod or as two joined chromatids. You need the stage and the relationship between the structures before deciding what the picture means.
For any diagram, first ask: how many chromosome types are shown, how many sets are present, and which structures are homologues? Only then consider replication.

lessons.title: The cell cycle and DNA replication
lessons.question: How does a cell prepare its genetic material before division?
lessons.goal: Explain G1, S, G2, mitosis and cytokinesis, connecting DNA replication with later inheritance by daughter cells.
lessons.prior: Ploidy counts chromosome sets. Copying a chromosome does not yet separate the copies into different cells.

terms.meaning: The ordered sequence of growth, DNA replication and division in a dividing cell.
terms.example: A cell grows, copies DNA, prepares for division and then divides.
terms.importantDistinction: Not every cell continuously cycles; some leave the active cycle.
terms.misconception: Every cell divides at the same constant rate.

terms.meaning: The G1, S and G2 parts of the cycle between divisions.
terms.example: A cell carries out metabolism and replicates its DNA before mitosis.
terms.importantDistinction: Interphase is active preparation and function, not a period with no activity.
terms.misconception: Interphase is an inactive resting period.

terms.meaning: The part of interphase during which DNA is replicated.
terms.example: Each chromosome is copied before its chromatids are separated.
terms.importantDistinction: DNA amount increases without an immediate doubling of chromosome number.
terms.misconception: S phase immediately doubles the chromosome count.

terms.meaning: The two replicated copies of a chromosome before their separation.
terms.example: Two copied DNA structures remain associated at the centromere region.
terms.importantDistinction: After separation, each chromatid is counted as an individual chromosome.
terms.misconception: Sister chromatids are maternal and paternal homologues.

sections: Interphase contains different kinds of work

During G1, a cell grows and carries out its normal activities. During S phase, it replicates its DNA. During G2, it continues preparing for division, including producing and organizing materials needed for chromosome movement. Together G1, S and G2 make up interphase.

Interphase is not inactivity. Many observed cells are in interphase because it occupies much of the cycle. The proportion of cells seen in each stage can provide evidence about relative time spent there, if the sampled population and observation method are appropriate.
Replication prepares two copies for distribution

In S phase, each chromosome's DNA is copied. The replicated chromosome consists of two sister chromatids associated at the centromere region. This provides copies that can later be distributed to daughter cells.

Keep chromosome number and DNA amount separate. A human body cell in G1 normally has 46 chromosomes. After S phase, before the sister chromatids separate, it still has 46 chromosomes but now has 92 chromatids. The DNA amount has doubled.

The X-shaped drawing is a simplified way of showing a condensed replicated chromosome. DNA is not necessarily condensed into that shape throughout S phase. A drawing can make relationships clearer without being a literal image of every stage.
Division has nuclear and cytoplasmic parts

Mitosis distributes replicated chromosomes into two nuclei. Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, producing separate daughter cells. These processes are coordinated but not identical. A cell can divide its nucleus without immediately completing cytoplasmic division.

Cell-cycle checkpoints help regulate whether a cell continues through the cycle. If regulation fails, uncontrolled division can contribute to cancer. “Dividing quickly” and “cancer” are not synonyms: normal growth and repair can also involve rapid cell division.
Follow the sequence as a preparation-and-distribution process. Replication supplies copies before mitosis separates them; cytokinesis then establishes separate cells.

lessons.title: Reading chromosome number and DNA amount
lessons.question: Why can two cells have the same chromosome number but different DNA amounts?
lessons.goal: Count chromosomes and chromatids through replication and separation, stating whether a count applies to a whole cell or one future nucleus.
lessons.prior: After S phase, sister chromatids remain joined until they separate. Each separated chromatid becomes a chromosome.

terms.meaning: The count of individual chromosomes in a specified cell or nucleus.
terms.example: A diploid model cell retains four chromosomes after replication until sister chromatids separate.

terms.meaning: The quantity of DNA in the specified cell or nucleus.
terms.example: The DNA quantity doubles during S phase before the cell divides.

terms.misconception: DNA amount is always equal to the number of chromosome sets.

terms.meaning: The mitotic stage in which sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles.

sections: Ask three questions before you count

First identify the stage. Has DNA replicated, and have sister chromatids separated? Next identify the boundary: are you counting the whole cell, one nucleus, or the chromosomes moving toward one pole? Finally state the quantity: chromosomes, chromatids or DNA amount.

Many errors come from answering a different question than the one asked. “Eight” can be correct for chromatids but incorrect for chromosomes in the same model cell. A count without its quantity and boundary is incomplete.
Use a small diploid model

Consider a cell with 2n = 4. In G1 it contains four unreplicated chromosomes, each with one DNA molecule. After S phase it still contains four chromosomes, now represented by eight chromatids. DNA amount has doubled.

During mitotic anaphase, the sister chromatids separate. Each is now a chromosome. The still-undivided cell therefore briefly contains eight chromosomes, with four moving toward each pole. After mitosis and cytokinesis, each daughter cell contains four chromosomes.

Do not interpret the temporary whole-cell count of eight as proof that the normal daughter cells have doubled their ploidy. The separated groups are being distributed into two cells. The scope of the count explains the apparent change.
Keep diagrams consistent with their meaning

A joined pair of rods or an X often represents one replicated chromosome. Two differently coloured X shapes of corresponding size may represent a replicated homologous pair: two chromosomes and four chromatids. The colour key should identify parental origin, not create a new counting rule.
Use centromere separation rather than counting every visible arm. A replicated chromosome with two chromatids can have four visible arms, but that does not make it four chromosomes.

A useful final check is conservation of the copied genetic material. Normal mitosis distributes one copy of each chromosome type to each daughter cell; it does not selectively discard one whole parental set.

lessons.title: Mitosis: chromosome movement through the stages
lessons.question: How does mitosis give two nuclei a matching chromosome complement?
lessons.goal: Trace prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, connecting visible events with accurate chromosome distribution.
lessons.prior: DNA replication has already occurred before normal mitosis. Sister chromatids are copies of one chromosome.

terms.meaning: The mitotic stage in which chromosomes condense and the division machinery becomes organized.
terms.example: Condensed replicated chromosomes become visible as spindle structures develop.
terms.importantDistinction: DNA replication precedes prophase in the normal cycle.
terms.misconception: The cell first copies its DNA during prophase.

terms.example: Replicated chromosomes line up individually across the middle of the cell.

sections: Prepare and align the chromosomes

During prophase, replicated chromosomes condense and the spindle becomes organized. The nuclear envelope breaks down as division proceeds, allowing spindle microtubules to interact with chromosome attachment regions. Some accounts distinguish part of this interval as prometaphase; the four-stage model groups these events for learning.

During metaphase, replicated chromosomes align individually along the equator of the cell. The two sister chromatids are connected to opposite spindle poles. This arrangement makes it possible to separate one copy toward each future daughter nucleus.
Separate copies, not homologous pairs
During anaphase, sister chromatids separate. Each becomes an individual chromosome and moves toward its assigned pole. The important event is separation of the copies made during S phase.

Mitosis does not normally pair maternal and paternal homologues into tetrads and separate those pairs as meiosis I does. A diploid cell uses mitosis to preserve the chromosome complement in the two daughter nuclei.

If a diagram uses two colours for parental origin, each normal mitotic daughter receives both parental contributions. Do not place all maternal chromosomes in one daughter and all paternal chromosomes in the other.
Finish nuclear organization

During telophase, chromosomes arrive at opposite poles, become less condensed and are enclosed by forming nuclear envelopes. The spindle breaks down. Cytokinesis then completes or overlaps the separation into daughter cells, depending on the cell type.

The sequence is often abbreviated PMAT: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. The abbreviation is useful only when connected with the events. In a new image, locate condensed chromosomes, their alignment, their separation or the forming nuclei.

Normal mitosis produces daughter nuclei with matching chromosome complements. Mutations or division errors can introduce differences, so “identical” describes the expected genetic distribution, not a guarantee against every possible change.

lessons.title: Cytokinesis, growth and tissue maintenance
lessons.question: How does division produce separate cells and support a multicellular body?
lessons.goal: Compare plant and animal cytokinesis, explain growth and repair, and distinguish normal cell-cycle control from uncontrolled division.
lessons.prior: Mitosis produces two nuclear chromosome groups. Separate cells also require division of the cytoplasm.

sections: Animal and plant cells divide differently

In an animal cell, a contractile ring helps constrict the cell surface. The resulting cleavage furrow deepens until the cytoplasm is separated. Each daughter cell receives a nucleus and cytoplasmic components.

A plant cell has a rigid cell wall, so it cannot complete division by the same inward pinching process. Vesicles gather and fuse near the cell middle, forming a cell plate. This partition expands and contributes to the new membranes and wall separating the daughter cells.

In both cases, the goal is separation into cells. The physical method differs because of cell structure. The word cytokinesis identifies the cytoplasmic process, not one specific shape of a dividing cell.
Division supports growth and replacement

A multicellular body grows partly by increasing cell number. Mitosis and cytokinesis also replace cells lost through normal wear and support repair after injury. Different tissues vary in how frequently their cells divide and in their ability to regenerate.

Stem cells can retain a capacity for division and produce cells that become specialized. This does not mean every body cell can form every tissue. The developmental potential of a stem cell depends on the type and its context.
A cell culture or tissue sample can help investigate division, but a visible increase in cell number alone does not show that a complete functional organ has been repaired.
Control matters as much as the capacity to divide

Checkpoints and signalling systems help regulate the cell cycle. They can delay division when conditions are unsuitable or DNA is damaged. Changes to genes involved in these controls can allow uncontrolled proliferation and contribute to cancer.

Telomeres are protective regions at chromosome ends. They shorten during many somatic-cell divisions and are involved in limitations on continued proliferation. Telomere length is not a simple personal countdown clock, and not every cell has the same maintenance mechanisms.
Compare outcomes using evidence: organized replacement supports tissue function; uncontrolled division can disrupt it. The rate of division by itself does not provide a complete diagnosis.

sections: Replication happens once before the two divisions

Meiosis begins after DNA replication. A diploid cell therefore has replicated chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids. It will undergo two divisions, but it does not perform another full round of DNA replication between them.

During prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair through synapsis. Each paired unit contains two replicated homologues and four chromatids, so it is called a tetrad. This organized pairing allows interactions, including crossing over, between corresponding regions of non-sister chromatids.
Arrange pairs, then separate homologues

At metaphase I, homologous pairs align at the equator. Their orientation relative to other pairs can vary. A replicated maternal homologue faces one pole and its paternal partner faces the other, but different pairs can orient independently.
During anaphase I, the homologues separate. The sister chromatids of each chromosome normally remain joined. The event is therefore different from mitotic anaphase, which separates sister chromatids.
After this distribution, each future daughter receives one chromosome of each homologous pair. It has one set rather than two. That is the reduction in ploidy.
A haploid cell can still have paired chromatids

At the end of meiosis I, the cells are haploid because each contains one homologue of each type. Their chromosomes are still replicated. In a 2n = 4 model, each daughter has two chromosomes, each containing two chromatids.

Do not call these daughter cells diploid merely because their chromosomes look like X shapes. The X shape represents replication, not two homologous sets. Meiosis II will separate the sister chromatids.
This distinction is central: meiosis I reduces sets; meiosis II separates the remaining copies. You cannot identify ploidy reliably by the shape of one chromosome alone.

sections: Separate the copies that remain

After meiosis I, each daughter cell has one chromosome of each type, but each chromosome still has two chromatids. Meiosis II separates these remaining copies. There is no normal full S phase between the divisions.

At metaphase II, chromosomes align individually in each cell. During anaphase II, sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles. Telophase II and cytokinesis establish the final haploid products.

The chromosome movements resemble mitosis, but the starting cells have one set of homologues rather than two. Because crossing over may have occurred, the chromatids that separate are not necessarily genetically identical over their whole lengths.
Check the final counts

In a 2n = 4 starting model, each cell after meiosis I has two replicated chromosomes. After meiosis II, each product has two unreplicated chromosomes. It remains haploid, n = 2. Meiosis II does not halve the number of chromosome types again.

The complete meiotic process usually produces four haploid nuclear products from one diploid precursor. Each contains a chromosome of every type needed for a haploid set. Random assortment and recombination create genetic differences among those products.
Functional gametes are not always four equal cells

During spermatogenesis, meiotic products can differentiate into four sperm. Their shape and cell contents are modified for their role in fertilization. A spermatid is not yet a fully mature sperm simply because meiosis has ended.

During oogenesis, cytoplasmic division is unequal. Most cytoplasm is retained in one large cell, while polar bodies receive other chromosome complements and little cytoplasm. This concentrates cellular resources in the future egg. In humans, the secondary oocyte normally completes meiosis II in connection with fertilization.
Distinguish four nuclear products from four equally functional gametes. The patterns of cytoplasm allocation and differentiation affect what the products become.

lessons.title: Crossing over and independent assortment
lessons.question: How can meiosis create different genetic combinations?
lessons.goal: Explain crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilization, keeping chromosome sets complete.
lessons.prior: Homologues can carry different alleles. Their orientation at metaphase I affects which combinations enter gametes.

terms.meaning: Exchange of corresponding DNA segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I.
terms.example: A chromatid contains segments derived from both parental homologues.

sections: Crossing over changes combinations within chromosomes

During prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair closely. Corresponding segments can be exchanged between non-sister chromatids. Because the homologues may carry different alleles, the exchange can produce chromatids with new combinations of parental variants.

The exchange normally occurs between corresponding regions. It should not be drawn as random loss of large unmatched chromosome pieces. A schematic can use two colours to track parental origin, but each resulting chromosome still needs the appropriate set of gene regions.
Crossing over reshuffles existing information. Mutation is a change in DNA sequence that can produce a new allele; these mechanisms are related to variation but are not the same event.
Different chromosome pairs orient independently

At metaphase I, one pair's orientation does not determine another pair's orientation. A gamete can therefore receive a mixture of maternal and paternal homologues. It does not normally receive an exclusively maternal set or exclusively paternal set as a rule.

For n independently assorting chromosome pairs, 2 to the power n gives the number of possible chromosome combinations from assortment alone. For a 2n = 4 model, n = 2, so 2² = 4 possible combinations. This counts types of possible combinations, not the number of cells made by one division.
For humans, n = 23, giving 2²³ = 8,388,608 possible combinations before including crossing over. The number illustrates why chromosome-set organization creates extensive variation.
Fertilization adds another combination step

A sperm and egg then combine by fertilization. Each may carry a different allele combination. Independent assortment, crossing over and random fertilization together make genetically different offspring possible.
The “independent” model has limits. Genes close together on one chromosome may travel together unless crossing over separates them. Chapter 17 will connect that linkage to inheritance ratios.
When explaining variation, name the mechanism and what it changes. Do not claim a process creates extra chromosome types when it actually rearranges which versions are inherited together.

lessons.title: Comparing mitosis and meiosis
lessons.question: How do chromosome movements explain the different outcomes?
lessons.goal: Compare replication, pairing, divisions, ploidy and genetic similarity in mitosis and meiosis.
lessons.prior: Mitosis separates sister chromatids; meiosis I separates homologues and meiosis II separates chromatids.

terms.meaning: A body cell other than a gamete or its germ-line precursor context.
terms.example: Skin cells contribute to body tissues rather than fertilizing an egg.
terms.importantDistinction: Many somatic cells use mitosis, but not all divide continuously.
terms.misconception: Somatic cell means only a sperm or egg.

terms.meaning: The lineage of cells that gives rise to gametes.
terms.example: Precursor cells in reproductive tissue ultimately contribute genetic information to offspring.

terms.meaning: Nuclear division that normally preserves chromosome number in daughter nuclei.
terms.example: A diploid precursor produces two nuclei each retaining two chromosome sets.

terms.meaning: A two-division process after one DNA replication that reduces chromosome sets and generates haploid products.

terms.importantDistinction: Meiosis is not simply two independent cycles of mitosis with replication before each.

sections: Begin with the purpose of chromosome distribution

Mitosis preserves the chromosome complement when a cell divides. It supports growth, replacement and asexual reproduction in many eukaryotes. A diploid cell normally makes diploid daughter nuclei; a haploid cell can make haploid daughter nuclei by mitosis.

Meiosis reduces chromosome sets in sexual life cycles. The reduction allows fertilization to restore a diploid set without chromosome number doubling at every generation. A diploid precursor undergoes one replication and two divisions.
Compare the mechanism before the outcome

Before both processes, DNA replication creates sister chromatids. In mitosis, chromosomes align individually and sister chromatids separate in one nuclear division. The result is normally two nuclei with matching chromosome complements.

In meiosis I, homologues pair, may exchange segments and then separate. In meiosis II, the sister chromatids separate without another full replication. The result is usually four haploid nuclear products, with genetic differences arising from assortment and recombination.
The presence of spindle fibres or condensed chromosomes alone does not distinguish the processes. Look for homologous pairing, which units separate and how chromosome sets change.
Connect a changed mechanism to a changed outcome

If a question shows two products, do not automatically choose mitosis; it may show only the end of meiosis I. Likewise, four pictures may show four stages of one process rather than four final cells. Read what each image represents.

To compare fairly, use the same starting chromosome model. For 2n = 4, normal mitosis produces two 2n = 4 nuclei. Complete meiosis produces haploid products with n = 2. Explain how the separation events produce these outcomes.
“Identical” is a useful expected pattern in normal mitosis, but mutations can occur. “Different” in meiosis concerns genetic combinations, not an instruction to remove essential chromosome types.

lessons.title: Nondisjunction and chromosome abnormalities
lessons.question: How do segregation errors change gamete chromosome numbers?
lessons.goal: Predict products of nondisjunction in meiosis I or II and distinguish aneuploidy from a change in whole chromosome sets.
lessons.prior: Normal meiosis I separates homologues; normal meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

terms.meaning: Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate properly during division.
terms.example: Both members intended for different products move into one product.
terms.importantDistinction: The outcome depends on which division and chromosome are affected.

sections: Track the affected chromosome separately

Nondisjunction occurs when chromosomes that should separate fail to do so. In meiosis I, a homologous pair may move together instead of separating. In meiosis II, sister chromatids may fail to separate in one of the cells.

To solve the problem, track one affected chromosome type through the divisions. Keep all other types behaving normally unless the question says otherwise. Mark which product receives both copies and which receives none.
Compare first-division and second-division errors

If a homologous pair fails to separate in meiosis I and meiosis II otherwise proceeds normally, all four final products have an abnormal number for that chromosome type. Two have an extra chromosome, n + 1, and two are missing one, n − 1.

If meiosis I is normal but sister chromatids fail to separate in one cell during meiosis II, two products can remain normal. The affected cell produces one n + 1 product and one n − 1 product. The other cell produces two normal n products.
These predictions assume one specified error and otherwise normal divisions. Multiple errors can produce other patterns, so do not apply the simplified pattern without checking the question.
Fertilization converts a gamete error into a zygote count
An n + 1 gamete joining a normal n gamete produces a 2n + 1 zygote, a trisomic complement for one chromosome. An n − 1 gamete joining a normal gamete produces 2n − 1, a monosomic complement.
An extra copy of one chromosome differs from an extra complete set. Trisomy 21, for example, concerns chromosome 21, not three copies of every chromosome. Polyploidy refers to additional whole sets.

A karyotype can identify many count abnormalities. The detailed effects depend on the chromosome and biological context; a schematic should not be treated as a complete prediction of a person's abilities or health.

sections: Classify the mechanism, not the species name

In asexual reproduction, offspring form without fusion of gametes. Budding in hydra and vegetative reproduction in plants are examples. Eukaryotic asexual reproduction often uses mitosis, maintaining the genetic complement of the parent lineage.

Sexual reproduction combines gametic contributions. Meiosis and fertilization create opportunities for new combinations of alleles. Some organisms use both sexual and asexual strategies at different times, so one familiar species name does not always determine the answer.
Different strategies have different trade-offs

Asexual reproduction can establish offspring without finding a mate and can preserve a successful genotype. However, genetically similar descendants may share vulnerabilities when conditions change. Mutation can still create differences, so clones are not permanently immune to variation.

Sexual reproduction can produce more varied allele combinations, potentially increasing the range of responses within offspring. It also involves costs such as gamete production and, in many organisms, finding or interacting with a mate. Neither strategy is universally best in every environment.

Parthenogenesis involves development from an unfertilized egg. Because different organisms use different cellular mechanisms, read the supplied life-cycle information before assigning ploidy or claiming all resulting offspring are identical.
Bacteria transfer DNA and divide by different processes

Bacteria reproduce by binary fission, copying genetic material and dividing the cell. They do not have a membrane-bound nucleus, so this is not nuclear mitosis with the same chromosome-stage sequence used for eukaryotes.

Bacteria can also exchange genetic material. During conjugation, direct contact can transfer DNA such as a plasmid. This changes genetic content but is not itself the production of an additional cell. Division and genetic exchange are different events.
Use the number of cells and the movement of DNA as separate observations. A diagram showing a connection between two cells may show exchange, not two gametes fusing.

sections: Use three rules through any diagram

Mitosis normally preserves ploidy. Meiosis reduces a diploid complement to haploid. Fertilization combines haploid gametic complements to form a diploid zygote. These rules help you interpret an unfamiliar life cycle without memorizing every species illustration.

Look for the arrows where chromosome sets change. A 2n-to-n transition suggests meiosis in the standard model. Fusion of two n cells to make 2n identifies fertilization. Growth from n to n or 2n to 2n commonly involves mitosis.
Follow a plant’s two multicellular stages

A diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores through meiosis. A spore develops by mitosis into a haploid gametophyte. The gametophyte then produces haploid gametes by mitosis. When gametes fuse, the diploid zygote grows by mitosis into a new sporophyte.

The surprising step for learners is gamete production by mitosis in the gametophyte. The parent stage is already haploid, so another reduction division is not needed. The meiotic products in this plant cycle are spores, not the final gametes.
Spores and gametes therefore have different roles. A spore can grow into a multicellular stage without fusion. A gamete contributes to the next diploid stage through fertilization.
The most visible stage depends on the organism

In mosses, the familiar green plant is usually the gametophyte, while the sporophyte remains attached to it. In conifers, the familiar tree is the sporophyte; the gametophytes are much smaller and develop in association with reproductive structures.

Do not label the largest structure diploid merely because it is large. Use the life-cycle arrows and the chromosome information. An unfamiliar organism may also alternate sexual and asexual reproduction without following the same plant pattern.
When answering, state the evidence: “These two haploid cells fuse, so this arrow represents fertilization.” That is stronger than guessing from a familiar-looking shape.

extension.title: Cell division and restoring tissue function
extension.question: Would making more sensory cells be enough to restore hearing?
sections: Replacement and function

Damage to sensory hair cells can impair hearing. A proposed repair approach might try to stimulate cell division or produce replacement cells. Increasing cell number is only one requirement: cells must also have the right structure, location and connections.

Consider a hypothetical culture in which treated cells divide more frequently and acquire hair-cell-like projections. The result supports an increase in cell number and a change in appearance. It does not yet establish sound detection or useful signalling to the nervous system.
Evidence beyond appearance

A stronger claim would require tests of mechanical sensitivity, appropriate neural communication and controlled growth. A cell that divides indefinitely would not automatically be a successful replacement.
The case connects cell-cycle control with specialization. It is a paper analysis, not a recommendation to attempt a treatment or manipulate biological samples.

sections: One counting method across the chapter

Identify homologues, sister chromatids and chromosome sets separately. DNA replication increases DNA amount while chromatids remain associated. Chromatid separation changes the number of independently counted chromosomes within the still-undivided cell. Always state whether the count refers to a whole cell, a pole or a daughter nucleus.
The same approach works for a small 2n = 4 model and a human 2n = 46 cell. The model simplifies the number of structures, not the underlying rules.
Mechanisms explain outcomes

Mitosis distributes copied chromosomes and normally preserves ploidy. Meiosis separates homologues and then chromatids, reducing sets while creating new combinations. Nondisjunction changes the count of a chromosome type when segregation fails.

In a life cycle, follow the arrows where sets change. Meiosis and fertilization balance the reduction and restoration of ploidy. Mitosis can occur in haploid or diploid stages; the largest visible body is not automatically diploid.
